title: Sacred blood, read in context
hookLine: a hadith naming three narrow cases for a court, which scholars discuss at length, and whose heart is how sacred a life is
tomorrow: say it, or stay quiet? there's a one-line test. what is it?
last: READ IT WITH THE SCHOLARS · AS MUCH AS YOU CAN · CLEAN FOOD, OPEN DOOR

cards: In a hospital, when a heart stops, an alarm goes out and people run, from every floor. Nobody stops to ask who the patient is first. Yesterday's question asked for the heart of a hard hadith about life and death.
Ibn Mas'ud reports the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, saying that the blood of a Muslim is not lawful except in one of three cases.
Read it the way the scholars did, and the weight falls on the first words: not lawful.

teach.h: THREE NARROW CASES, FOR A COURT.
teach.b: The three, as the hadith names them: a married person who commits adultery, a life for a life, and one who leaves the religion and separates from the community.
Classical scholars treated all three as matters for a court alone, never for a private person, under strict conditions of proof.
On the last, some scholars read the hadith's own words, separates from the community, as about turning against the community, not belief by itself, and scholars still discuss it.
But before any exception, the hadith sets the rule: a life is not lawful to take.

The Qur'an says the rule out loud, in Pickthall's words: "whosoever killeth a human being for other than manslaughter or corruption in the earth, it shall be as if he had killed all mankind, and whoso saveth the life of one, it shall be as if he had saved the life of all mankind."
One to tell a friend tonight: the same verse says this was decreed for the Children of Israel, Moses' people.
One life weighed as all humankind.

how: Muslim scholars teach this hadith with its legal commentaries, stressing that its cases belong only to a court with strict conditions of proof, and pair it with Qur'an 5:32 on the worth of a single life.

practice: On a scrap of paper, copy one line by hand, slowly: whoso saveth the life of one, it shall be as if he had saved the life of all mankind. Then hold in mind the people whose lives are in danger today, near or far.
If you pray, you can pray for them; if not, keep them in mind with care until the sit ends.

wordCard.voice: Sacred blood: a life that is not lawful to take. The hadith sets that rule first, then names its narrow exceptions for a court.
